parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Invention of Television

The question “Who invented television?” is simple enough, but the answer is surprisingly controversial. No single person was responsible for producing what we think of as television today. Instead, its development depended on the work of several inventors, whose ideas often built on one another.

One of the earliest important contributors was the German inventor Paul Nipkow. He devised a method of “scanning” an image using a spinning disk with a spiral of small pinholes. As the disk rotated at high speed, each hole allowed light reflected from the object being photographed to fall on a selenium cell. The amount of voltage generated by the cell depended on the amount of light it received, and one complete rotation of the disk produced one frame of “video”. At the receiving end, the process was reversed: a similar disk spun in synchronisation while a neon lamp responded to changes in voltage and projected the image onto a screen. Although Nipkow created the disk and acquired a patent for his invention, he did not create the apparatus to project images. The patent eventually expired after 15 years, as the work attracted no interest during that period. His ideas were later incorporated into practical television systems, and Nipkow became a celebrated scientist in Germany. Eventually, however, the mechanical nature of his disk caused the system to fade into obscurity with the arrival of the cathode ray tube.

Another German scientist, Arthur Korn, also contributed to the technological foundations on which later television systems depended. His early work focused on visual telegraphic transmission and made use of advances in amplification tube technology. In 1906, he transmitted a picture of the German Crown Prince over a distance of 1,800 kilometres, and in 1923 he sent a picture of the Pope across the Atlantic. Korn’s work helped to develop Nipkow’s ideas, which in turn contributed to Baird’s later breakthroughs. His technology also found practical applications outside broadcasting: from 1928, the German police used it to transmit photographs and fingerprints.

It was partly on these earlier developments that the Scotsman John Logie Baird built some of the first practical television systems. Baird had shown signs of inventive ingenuity from an early stage, once setting up a telephone exchange to connect his house with those of nearby friends. His interest in television began in 1903 after he read a German book describing the photoelectric properties of selenium. In 1873, this element was discovered to have the capacity to generate an electric current proportional to the amount of light applied to it. While working in Hastings, England, Baird constructed an experimental apparatus from an old hatbox bought in a second-hand shop, a pair of scissors, some needles, bicycle-light lenses and an old tea chest. His system made use of Nipkow’s disk and also drew on Korn’s earlier work, bringing together several developments that had preceded him.

In February 1924, Baird demonstrated moving silhouette images on a “television”. Later that year, after almost destroying his house and nearly killing himself with an electric shock, he moved to London, where he gave the first public display of his invention. On 2 October 1925, he used his office assistant, William Taynton, as the subject of a transmission. Taynton became the first person to be televised moving and in full tonal range. Baird later demonstrated what were claimed to be the first colour television images on 3 July 1928, although the identity of the inventor of colour television is also disputed. In the same year, he transmitted television pictures across the Atlantic for the first time. Although Baird was well known for his invention, he gained further fame by refusing a £100,000 offer for shares in his company—an enormous sum at the time. He reportedly said that he would not be able to sleep at night knowing that he had so much money.

Baird, however, was not the only person who could claim an early breakthrough in television. The American inventor Charles Francis Jenkins, already well known for inventing the motion-picture projector, transmitted a silhouette picture from one room to another in 1922. He later founded a broadcasting company in 1928, but the financial crash of 1929 forced him out of business. Most accounts place Baird’s first public television demonstration a couple of years before Jenkins’s, although this chronology remains disputed in some sources.

Meanwhile, a different approach to television was emerging in the United States: electronic television. In 1927, Philo Farnsworth successfully demonstrated an electronic television system in San Francisco. His system used a television camera to break a picture into a series of electrical lines. These were transmitted so rapidly that the human eye would merge them into an image. Farnsworth’s own invention, the image dissector, then converted the electrical information back into a picture. The Russian inventor Vladimir Zworykin subsequently built on this work. His designs were eventually adopted by the BBC in the United Kingdom to replace Baird’s mechanical system.

It is therefore plain that the identity of the inventor of television remains controversial. The technology emerged from a succession of related discoveries rather than from the work of one person alone. Some inventors provided important mechanical principles, others advanced the transmission of images, and still others developed practical mechanical or electronic television systems. In many cases, the answer to the question “Who invented television?” simply depends on the country of the person answering it.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Speaking of Nothing

Why we talk about the weather and other trivia

A

Some workers are happier in their jobs than others, but this is not only to do with the work itself. Consider security guards, truck drivers and salespeople: year after year, these occupations appear on lists of the unhappiest careers. It is true that many factors can make a job cheerless, including unusual hours, low pay and a lack of opportunities for advancement. However, these three types of work stand out for another reason: they involve either little conversation or obligatory small talk that is largely superficial. Typical subjects include the weather, holiday destinations and food. Psychologists have long argued that connecting with others through meaningful exchanges is central to well-being, but exactly how much conversation we require is still under investigation.

B

Matthias R. Mehl and Simine Vazire of the University of Arizona in the United States wanted to investigate the types of conversations people have. Their team used a device to record short verbal exchanges periodically while participants went about their daily activities. The researchers monitored undergraduates for four days, then classified each recorded conversation as either ‘small talk’ or ‘substantive’. They found that people who had more substantive conversations were more likely to report feeling happy and fulfilled overall. In fact, the happiest students had roughly twice as many substantive conversations as the unhappiest ones. Small talk, meanwhile, accounted for only 10 per cent of the conversations of the happiest students, compared with almost 30 per cent among the least content.

C

However, small talk still has a role to play. Rather than conveying information, scientists believe that it can promote social bonding. Ipek Kulahci and her team at University College Cork in Ireland examined the relationship between vocal exchanges and grooming in lemurs. The researchers found that the animals reserved their call-and-response conversations, the equivalent of human chitchat, for those they groomed most often. This suggests that small talk can help maintain closeness with familiar companions rather than serving merely as a way of managing awkward exchanges with strangers. It appears that, even among animals, vocal exchanges can indicate strong social bonds between group members.

D

Connecting with others seems to increase happiness, yet strangers in close proximity routinely ignore one another. To examine the experience of connecting with strangers, psychologists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder of the University of Chicago gave volunteers different instructions about whether to talk to fellow commuters on their regular train journey to work—something they would normally avoid. Those told to chat with others reported a more pleasant journey than those told to ‘enjoy your solitude’ or behave as they normally would. All the volunteers who initiated conversations reported a positive reaction from the people they spoke to. Yet the participants had predicted precisely the opposite: they had expected the other commuters to prefer being left alone.

E

When we buy a cup of coffee at a café, we sometimes chat with the service staff, but on other occasions we say as little as possible in order to save time. Every day, we have opportunities to transform potentially impersonal exchanges into genuine social interactions. In other words, treating a service provider as we would an acquaintance might make us happier. In a study by Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, people who interacted socially with a server in a coffee shop felt better emotionally than those who were in a rush to get everything done. As well as feeling happier, the first group had a stronger sense of belonging. Similar results have emerged in other settings. When volunteers broke the silence in an art gallery to chat with other visitors, those visitors felt happier and more connected to the paintings than people who were not approached. The pleasure of connection also appears to be contagious: in a laboratory waiting room, participants who were spoken to reported experiences that were just as positive as those of the people instructed to start the conversation.

F

Of course, some of us are better than others at small talk. In a study by Todd Kashdan and his team at George Mason University in the United States, people rated as ‘less curious about all aspects of life’ had difficulty starting conversations on their own. However, they were more successful at building closeness with others when supplied with topics that encouraged people to open up about themselves and their lives. By contrast, people judged to be ‘curious’ needed no help moving from ordinary subjects such as favourite holidays to more personal areas of conversation. In another experiment, William Fleeson of Wake Forest University divided participants into two groups: those who were naturally outgoing and those who were more reserved in social situations. They were then instructed to behave in the opposite manner to their usual disposition. Participants reported more positive feelings when instructed to act extroverted than when instructed to act introverted. The overall conclusion, therefore, is that everyone can benefit from more conversation—the more meaningful, the better.

Why we talk about the weather and other trivia

A

Some workers are happier in their jobs than others, but this is not only to do with the work itself. Consider security guards, truck drivers and salespeople: year after year, these occupations appear on lists of the unhappiest careers. It is true that many factors can make a job cheerless, including unusual hours, low pay and a lack of opportunities for advancement. However, these three types of work stand out for another reason: they involve either little conversation or obligatory small talk that is largely superficial. Typical subjects include the weather, holiday destinations and food. Psychologists have long argued that connecting with others through meaningful exchanges is central to well-being, but exactly how much conversation we require is still under investigation.

B

Matthias R. Mehl and Simine Vazire of the University of Arizona in the United States wanted to investigate the types of conversations people have. Their team used a device to record short verbal exchanges periodically while participants went about their daily activities. The researchers monitored undergraduates for four days, then classified each recorded conversation as either ‘small talk’ or ‘substantive’. They found that people who had more substantive conversations were more likely to report feeling happy and fulfilled overall. In fact, the happiest students had roughly twice as many substantive conversations as the unhappiest ones. Small talk, meanwhile, accounted for only 10 per cent of the conversations of the happiest students, compared with almost 30 per cent among the least content.

C

However, small talk still has a role to play. Rather than conveying information, scientists believe that it can promote social bonding. Ipek Kulahci and her team at University College Cork in Ireland examined the relationship between vocal exchanges and grooming in lemurs. The researchers found that the animals reserved their call-and-response conversations, the equivalent of human chitchat, for those they groomed most often. This suggests that small talk can help maintain closeness with familiar companions rather than serving merely as a way of managing awkward exchanges with strangers. It appears that, even among animals, vocal exchanges can indicate strong social bonds between group members.

D

Connecting with others seems to increase happiness, yet strangers in close proximity routinely ignore one another. To examine the experience of connecting with strangers, psychologists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder of the University of Chicago gave volunteers different instructions about whether to talk to fellow commuters on their regular train journey to work—something they would normally avoid. Those told to chat with others reported a more pleasant journey than those told to ‘enjoy your solitude’ or behave as they normally would. All the volunteers who initiated conversations reported a positive reaction from the people they spoke to. Yet the participants had predicted precisely the opposite: they had expected the other commuters to prefer being left alone.

E

When we buy a cup of coffee at a café, we sometimes chat with the service staff, but on other occasions we say as little as possible in order to save time. Every day, we have opportunities to transform potentially impersonal exchanges into genuine social interactions. In other words, treating a service provider as we would an acquaintance might make us happier. In a study by Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, people who interacted socially with a server in a coffee shop felt better emotionally than those who were in a rush to get everything done. As well as feeling happier, the first group had a stronger sense of belonging. Similar results have emerged in other settings. When volunteers broke the silence in an art gallery to chat with other visitors, those visitors felt happier and more connected to the paintings than people who were not approached. The pleasure of connection also appears to be contagious: in a laboratory waiting room, participants who were spoken to reported experiences that were just as positive as those of the people instructed to start the conversation.

F

Of course, some of us are better than others at small talk. In a study by Todd Kashdan and his team at George Mason University in the United States, people rated as ‘less curious about all aspects of life’ had difficulty starting conversations on their own. However, they were more successful at building closeness with others when supplied with topics that encouraged people to open up about themselves and their lives. By contrast, people judged to be ‘curious’ needed no help moving from ordinary subjects such as favourite holidays to more personal areas of conversation. In another experiment, William Fleeson of Wake Forest University divided participants into two groups: those who were naturally outgoing and those who were more reserved in social situations. They were then instructed to behave in the opposite manner to their usual disposition. Participants reported more positive feelings when instructed to act extroverted than when instructed to act introverted. The overall conclusion, therefore, is that everyone can benefit from more conversation—the more meaningful, the better.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

Antibiotic Resistance

An antibiotic is a drug that kills or prevents the growth of bacteria. The term "antibiotic", coined by Selman Waksman, originally described only those antibiotics derived from living organisms, in contrast to "chemotherapeutic agents", which are purely synthetic. Currently, the term antibiotic is also applied to synthetic antimicrobials.

Overuse or misuse of antibiotics may result in the development of antibiotic resistance in the infecting organisms, similar to the development of pesticide resistance in insects. Doctor Iain Nicholson explains: "The concept of genetic selection requires that as close as possible to 100 per cent of the infecting organisms be killed off to avoid selection of resistance. If a small subset of the population survives the treatment and is allowed to multiply, the average susceptibility of this new population to the compound will be much lower than that of the original population, since they have descended from those few organisms that survived the original treatment."

Antibiotic resistance has become a serious problem in both developed and developing nations. In certain settings, such as hospitals, the rate of antibiotic resistance is so high today that the normal, low-cost antibiotics are virtually useless for the treatment of frequently seen infections. This leads to more common use of newer and more expensive compounds, which in turn leads to the rise of resistance to those drugs. Drug company spokesperson Emma Thompson explains the challenge facing the drug industry: "A continuous race to discover new and different antibiotics results in an attempt to keep humanity from losing ground in the battle against infection. The fear is that we will eventually fail to keep up in this race, and that people may again face life-threatening bacterial infections."

An example of antibiotic resistance is Staphylococcus aureus, which used to be treated successfully with penicillin in the 1940s and 1950s. At present, nearly all strains are resistant to penicillin, and many are resistant to other antibiotics, leaving only a narrow selection of drugs useful for treatment. The situation is worsened by the fact that genes coding for antibiotic resistance can be transferred between bacteria, making it possible for bacteria never exposed to an antibiotic to acquire resistance from those which have been.

Microbial resistance to antibiotics is a natural consequence of selective pressures placed on bacteria. However, humans have greatly accelerated the evolution of resistant bacteria through the overuse and misuse of antibiotics in the community. Government health official Georgina Haynes explains: "One of the major problems is when antibiotics are used to treat disorders for which they have no efficacy, such as the common cold or other viral complaints, and when they are used widely as prophylaxis rather than treatment, because this exposes more bacteria to selection for resistance." Similarly, in order to kill all the bacteria of an infection, antibiotics must be taken for a whole course and not stopped just when symptoms improve. The discoverer of penicillin himself, Alexander Fleming, warned the scientific community: "The administration of too small doses leads to the production of resistant strains of bacteria." This can happen due to patient ignorance and improper pharmacy practices, usually in the developing world. In developing countries, antibiotic prescriptions are often broken up. For example, in some Asian countries, it is common for pharmacies to sell as many tablets as the patient can afford, which may be only two or three. This is an insufficient dose to cure an infection and will only further contribute to the evolution of resistant strains of bacteria. Recent reports have also shown that containers of medicine from some African countries sometimes contain only half the drug content indicated on the label. This may be due to "counterfeit" medicines or improper storage, but tropical conditions, such as those often found in Africa, also readily cause degradation of medical compounds. Chenbo Okonkwa, a pharmaceutical wholesaler, describes the problem: "Although local regulations may require pharmacies to store drugs in air-conditioned premises, most undergo frequent power outages, and warehouses are rarely kept cool. Furthermore, unauthorised dealers rarely bother to follow official storage guidelines."

Another problem contributing to antibiotic resistance is that antibiotics are widely used in food-producing animals, which contributes to the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in them. These resistant bacteria can contaminate the foods that come from these animals, and people who consume these foods can develop antibiotic-resistant infections. This can be seen, for instance, in the fish farming industry. It is common to put upwards of 100,000 fish into each pen, which creates cramped and stressful conditions. This increases the susceptibility of fish to certain bacterial diseases, such as furunculosis. Furunculosis, an infection of the kidneys, is easily transmitted through water and so is devastating to fish farms. To combat the disease, antibiotics were added to fish food pellets, but these were unpalatable to the fish. The fish were already suffering from loss of appetite due to their infections, and so most of the antibiotics ended up at the bottom of the pens, allowing residual drugs to spread throughout the marine environment. Fish farmer Jo Hardwick explains that this is different now: "Today, vaccines are replacing the antibiotic pellets as a treatment for the disease, but unfortunately, most of the damage has already been done."

In conclusion, antibiotics must be used judiciously in both humans and animals, because both uses contribute to the emergence, persistence, and spread of resistant bacteria. Resistant bacteria in food-producing animals are of particular concern. Food animals serve as a reservoir of resistant pathogens and resistance mechanisms that can directly or indirectly result in antibiotic-resistant infections in humans. If people do not wish to be faced with an attack of all the diseases they thought they had conquered in the twentieth century, society has to change its approach to antibiotic use.
